items.note: A governor's claimed descent from Dhar Paramaras; author notes defeated Hindu royal family members were often converted under Muslim rule.
items.gloss: He said he was a descendant of the Paramaras of Dhar who had at some time gone to Uttar Pradesh. Not much is known about which Paramara ancestor accepted Islam, when, or why. Under Muslim rule there are countless cases where members of defeated Hindu royal families were converted.

items.note: 448 years after the first inscription (1080), in 1528 Udaypur lay in Chanderi sarkar, held by local occupiers appointed by the Mughals; author conjectures how.
items.gloss: 448 years after the year 1080 on Udaipur's first inscription, in 1528, when Firdaus Makani Babur was destroying Chanderi, Udaipur entered a bad period within that Chanderi sarkar, its new masters being local occupiers appointed by the Mughals. It may be that Muslims already in possession backed the new Mughal rulers at Agra and kept possession, or a new raider sat here after raising his flag over Chanderi.

items.note: Ruined palace complex shows Paramara architecture in every pillar and doorway; the mosque built inside the palace's square enclosure reuses Paramara pillar stones and was probably part of the palace, converted into a place of worship.
items.gloss: Every pillar, lintel and door of the ruined palace complex a little behind the temple is precious evidence of Paramara architecture. Feel the stones of the pillars of the mosque built in one part: they too point to the Paramaras. The mosque is also built within the palace's vast square complex. It must originally have been part of the palace, but after Muslim occupation this court-like structure was turned into a place of worship.

items.note: Prayers for Babur said near the palace ruins unnoticed by officials; an unlawful-occupation signboard stayed on part of the palace after Madhya Pradesh's formation.
items.gloss: Countless officials came, but none had an inkling that near the palace ruins prayers were repeatedly being offered for Babur. In Udaipur, in everyone's sight, an illegal-occupation signboard on a part of the palace hung since the formation of Madhya Pradesh. The occupiers had just packed up and left.

items.note: Despite the calamities, thousands kept coming daily for darshan at Nilakantheshwar Mahadev.
items.gloss: Even after all these disasters, thousands of 'kafirs' kept coming every day for darshan of Nilakantheshwar Mahadev.

items.note: A naib tehsildar issued a public eviction order against the Qazi who read prayers for Firdaus Makani.
items.gloss: How dare a naib tehsildar issue an open eviction order against the Qazi, who reads prayers for Firdaus Makani and also writes himself as Sayyid.

items.note: Until now Jahangir's farman held in Udaypur; Naib Tehsildar Dauji Ram Ahirwar's order.
items.gloss: Until now Jahangir's farman was in force here. Let us read this priceless document of contemporary history as it is. Because of this one paper Naib Tehsildar Dauji Ram Ahirwar has become immortal in history.

items.note: After the last Mughals were finished in India, a Mughal presence survived at Udaypur only through a Persian farman.
items.gloss: The last remnant of the Mughals in India was finished. But in Udaipur a Mughal remnant survived in the name of the Mughals on the strength of a Persian farman.

items.note: Vidisha described as a prosperous major town long before Udaypur; its past leads straight to Ashoka, married to a local woman 2300 years ago.
items.gloss: We had reached the district headquarters, historically a prosperous major city much earlier than Udaipur. Vidisha's past leads straight to Emperor Ashoka, who married a girl from here, 2300 years ago.

items.note: Vijay Mandir of Vidisha said to be built by Paramara king Naravarman, Udayaditya's successor; author conjectures young Naravarman lived at Udaypur during the temple's construction.
items.gloss: The most special thing in old Vidisha is the Vijay temple built by Paramara king Naravarman. In the Paramara genealogy Naravarman comes after Udayaditya; he was his successor. It is possible that young Naravarman lived in Udaipur at the time of building the Nilakantheshwar temple, and kept an inclination toward this region after ruling from Dhar.

items.note: Vidisha larger and older than Udaypur, known history reaching Mauryas; Sanchi stupas, Kalidasa's Meghaduta and Gupta remains.
items.gloss: Vidisha was a bigger and more ancient city than Udaipur, whose known history goes back easily to the Mauryas. Ashoka lived in Ujjain before becoming emperor. The Sanchi stupas near Vidisha began to be built then. Kalidasa's clouds travel through Vidisha in the Meghaduta. Then came the Gupta period, whose evidence is scattered around the region.

items.note: Vijay Mandir at Vidisha first razed in Iltutmish's attack; Minhaj Siraj gives the height as 105 gaz.
items.gloss: That temple was first razed to the ground in Shamsuddin Iltutmish's attack. The contemporary historian Minhaj Siraj wrote the height of this Bhilsa temple as 105 yards. Judging from its huge foundation, the height would have been just this.

items.note: Heliodorus's visit to Vidisha and conversion to Vaishnavism, recorded on the Khambaba pillar by the Betwa.
items.gloss: It was a memorable visit to a city where two thousand years ago a Greek ambassador came. Moved by the society and customs, he decided to accept Vaishnavism. It is an immortal episode recorded on a stone pillar on the Betwa, famed as Khambaba, once a garuda pillar before a temple. No trace of the temple remains, but Heliodorus's inscription can still be read on the pillar.

items.note: Imagined account of Heliodorus's time: Ashoka and Pushyamitra Shunga stories fresh, Sanchi stupas under construction, Mahendra and Sanghamitra visiting their mother.
items.gloss: When he first came, the stories of Magadha's Emperor Ashoka and Pushyamitra Shunga were very fresh. Stupas were still being built at Sanchi. Mahendra and Sanghamitra had come to meet their mother before leaving for Sri Lanka. The fragrance of the smoke of the Shungas' sacrificial altars freshened the air.

items.note: Heliodorus changed his religion and had it announced on a large pillar.
items.gloss: He gave his heart to Vidisha so much that he changed his religion. He had it formally announced inscribed on a large pillar so that history would know it well.

items.note: Imagined voice of Minhaj Siraj: the 105-gaz temple razed by Iltutmish, who then moved on to Ujjain; first Islamic armies to arrive.
items.gloss: It was a temple 105 yards high, visible from very far. Delhi's Sultan Shamsuddin Iltutmish has destroyed it. They looted the city and went toward Ujjain, where they will do the same to the Mahakal temple. For the first time Islamic armies have knocked here.

items.note: Boar-incarnation Vishnu on the Udayagiri rock, a 1500-year-old Gupta emperors' sacred mark.
items.gloss: Recognising Vishnu on that huge rock gave him relief. Vishnu stands proudly in his boar incarnation, hand on waist, Earth as a woman on his tusk; Vishnu has rescued the earth sunk in the deluge. A 1500-year-old sacred sign of the Gupta emperors in stone at Udayagiri.

items.note: Author states Udaypur's deep relation with Bhoja; Udayaditya became maharaja after him and likely prepared under his patronage (conjecture).
items.gloss: After all, Udaipur too has a deep relationship with Raja Bhoj. Udayaditya became maharaja after him. Bhoj must have been well aware of every outline of Udaipur's development. Udayaditya must have prepared himself for skilled governance with his rich interests under Bhoj's patronage.
